blocks.md: Cobb-Douglas is a recipe for how much an economy, or a firm, can produce from two ingredients: capital (machines, buildings, computers) and workers. It builds in three common-sense features. Double both ingredients and you double output. Each extra machine adds a little less than the one before, because there are only so many workers to run them. And capital always ends up earning the same fixed slice of total income — about a third in the US — however much of it there is. A separate productivity term stands for everything else that makes the ingredients productive: technology, know-how, how well the economy is organised.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is simple enough to solve by hand, yet it matches a real pattern — income shares that barely move over decades — so the Solow model, growth accounting and most textbook micro use it as the default.

$A$ is total factor productivity (TFP); $\alpha$ is the capital share. It is the $\sigma = 1$ member of the [CES Production Function](note:ces-production-function) family, but it is used so widely, and has so many convenient properties of its own, that it is worth knowing separately.

| Property | Statement | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Constant returns | $F(tK, tL) = tF(K,L)$ | Lets you write output per worker as a function of capital per worker ([Homogeneous Functions and Euler's Theorem](note:homogeneous-functions-and-eulers-theorem)) |
| Marginal products | $MPK = \alpha Y/K$, $MPL = (1-\alpha)Y/L$ | Competitive factor prices |
| **Constant factor shares** | $\frac{MPK\cdot K}{Y} = \alpha$, $\frac{MPL\cdot L}{Y} = 1-\alpha$ | The capital share can be read off national accounts (≈ 1/3) |
| Diminishing returns | $\partial MPK/\partial K < 0$ | Drives convergence in growth models ([Convexity and Concavity](note:convexity-and-concavity)) |
| Inada conditions | $MPK\to\infty$ as $K\to0$, $\to 0$ as $K\to\infty$ | Guarantees an interior steady state |
| Elasticity of substitution | $\sigma = 1$ | Factor shares do not move when relative prices change |
Divide by $L$: with $y = Y/L$ and $k = K/L$,
Output per worker depends only on capital per worker — a direct consequence of constant returns.

So with Cobb-Douglas, Hicks-neutral, capital-augmenting and labor-augmenting technology are observationally equivalent ([Factor-Augmenting Technology](note:factor-augmenting-technology)). If $A$ grows at $\gamma$, $\tilde{A}$ grows at $\gamma/(1-\alpha)$ ([Logarithms and Growth Rates](note:logarithms-and-growth-rates)).

- Treating $\alpha$ as a free parameter: under competition it equals capital's share of income.
- Forgetting the $1/(1-\alpha)$ when converting TFP growth into labor-augmenting growth.

- **Macro / growth**: the [Solow Growth Model](note:solow-growth-model), growth accounting ([Multivariable Chain Rule](note:multivariable-chain-rule)), the [Golden Rule Saving Rate](note:golden-rule-saving-rate) ($s = \alpha$).
- **Labor**: the $\sigma = 1$ benchmark against which the [Elasticity of Substitution](note:elasticity-of-substitution) between skill groups is tested.
- **Micro**: the workhorse utility and production function.
